title: Zepto beyond Groceries | How the grocery app became a shopping destination
body_markdown:
Zepto started as the fastest way to buy groceries, and grocery shoppers arrive knowing what they want: milk, atta, the biscuits they buy every week. We built for that. Compact cards showed a picture, name, pack size and price. Dense listings let you scan more products per scroll, and search took you to something you could already name.


Then we started selling T-shirts, makeup, air fryers, toys, skincare and a lot more.


Customers opened the app for these without a decision made. A T-shirt buyer compares fabric, fit, colour and size. An air fryer buyer weighs capacity and specs across models. Someone shopping for skincare may still be figuring out which product is right for them.


How different products require different attributes in the decision making


Getting these products to customers quickly wasn’t the only problem we were trying to solve. We also had to help them choose.


Fast delivery still mattered. But the decision now happened inside Zepto, and we had designed the app for people who showed up with it already made.


**That’s where the grocery experience stopped working.**


We spoke with roughly 300 customers across different persona and studied how people searched, browsed, carted and ordered in these categories over the last year. The gap showed up in six places, from discovering a category to receiving the order.


Six questions from ~300 customer conversations, in the order a purchase happens


On their own these looked like separate problems: discovery, conversion, merchandising, cart behaviour. But they pointed to the same gap.


We had built an experience that was very good at helping customers find something they already understood. Now we were asking it to help them decide what to buy.


That became the product problem we spent much of the next year working on.


> *Sizes came up in almost every apparel conversation. Customers said they didn’t want to open a product to find out whether it came in their size, because a T-shirt that doesn’t is not a product they need to look at. What we were treating as a detail on the product page, they were treating as the first filter.*


### What we built


We solved for each question that user had. Most of them change parts of the app that grocery shoppers never needed: a place to browse new categories, product cards built for comparison, and prices that show offers before checkout. The overview below maps each question to what we built, and the sections that follow take them in the same order.


How customer questions across the shopping journey shaped what we built.


### SuperMall


*New way to show customers what Zepto sells*


You can’t search for something you don’t know exists. Search helps only customers who already know what to type. Most customers think of Zepto as a grocery app, so they don’t think to search it for a hair dryer or a Bluetooth speaker. We could stock the product, price it well and deliver it in ten minutes, and still never make the sale.


We built **Super Mall** to give Fashion, Electronics, Beauty and Home a place customers could browse into, with no search query needed.


Super Mall — dedicated destination for the new categories


### Better Merchandising: Making the full range visible


Customers who reached a category still saw only a small part of it. Merchandising widgets kept surfacing the same few products, so a customer returning on a later visit found the same shelf and assumed that was all we had.


Adding more products wouldn’t have fixed this, because new products would have stayed as hidden as the ones we already stocked. We changed which products customers saw instead:


- Occasion-led collections, such as gifting or festive picks
- Age-led discovery for toys and kids’ products
- Widgets that swap out products a customer has already seen or skipped


The measure we cared about afterwards wasn’t how many products we had listed. It was how many of them customers actually reached. ATC share spread across a noticeably wider set of products instead of concentrating on the same few, and the share coming from our top 20 products fell meaningfully.


Same familiar experience but with fresh products every few sessions


### Category led search


*Redesigning search to help customers decide*


A customer who types “garbage bag” knows what they want, and a dense 3×3 grid gets them to it faster. A customer who types “T-shirt” is comparing colour, cut, material and fit, which nine thumbnails show poorly. In research, apparel shoppers told us they saw nine T-shirts on the screen and couldn’t tell one from the next. Some didn’t want to open a T-shirt to learn it wasn’t in their size.


**Choosing the grid for each query**


Home holds both “bedsheet” and “garbage bag.” Shoppers judge a bedsheet by how it looks and pick a garbage bag by size, so we couldn’t give Home a single layout. We tagged high-volume queries by intent instead, using signals such as how often customers opened product pages before adding to cart. We moved queries like “T-shirt” to a 2×2 grid with larger images, and queries like “garbage bag” kept the 3×3 grid.


Redesigned search layout, and the product cards


**Shortlisting details on the card**


A grocery card works with an image, name, pack size and price. A sunscreen card needs SPF and skin type. Earbuds need playback time. Apparel needs material and available sizes.


Sizes came up in almost every apparel conversation. Customers wanted to see which sizes were in stock before opening a product. If the T-shirt doesn’t come in their size, they had to tap into the page to learn that, and it wasted their time.


Most of these details already existed on the product page, so comparing ten products meant opening ten pages.


The bigger cards needed images in a new aspect ratio. Reshooting thousands of products would have held up the launch, so we used AI to extend the photos we already had.


We picked these using research / filter usage / most-viewed product page attributes, and left the rest on the product page. A phone has dozens of specs, and we left the rest on the product page.


Making the bigger purchase feel affordable via Best Price and EMI


### Showing the price customers pay


On a grocery card, the listed price is close to what you pay. That stopped being true for higher-ticket products. Product discounts, bank offers and coupons often brought the price down, but customers saw the lower number only after they added the product to cart.


The card is where a customer decides whether a product deserves a closer look. Someone who saw ₹1,000 and thought it too expensive scrolled past before any offer appeared. A customer comparing five air fryers compared them on prices they wouldn’t end up paying.


We followed a two-pronged approach to solve this problem:


- **Best Price:** Cards in browse and search show the lowest price a customer can get after applicable offers, and name the offer that unlocks it. If a product is listed at ₹1,000 and a bank offer takes it to ₹900, the card shows ₹900 and tells the customer how to get it. Customers now compare products on the price they can pay, instead of discovering the discount at checkout.
- **EMI on cards and product pages:** Customers are used to seeing EMI and no-cost EMI when they buy expensive products online. Most didn’t expect it on Zepto, so they didn’t look for it, even when it was available. The few who found it did so at payment, if they got that far. We now show the monthly amount on cards and product pages. A customer looking at a ₹10,000 purchase also sees ₹656 a month, and can judge whether it fits their monthly budget before ruling the product out.


Making the bigger purchase feel affordable via Best Price and EMI


> *The offers were always there. The customer just had to work to find them, and the point at which they gave up was earlier than the point at which we were showing them.*


### Letting customers decide over several visits


Customers kept products they weren’t ready to buy in the cart, so they could find them again later. When they needed the cart for an immediate order, they removed those products and lost track of them.


For purchases that take more than one visit, we built:


- **Wishlist.** Customers save a product without adding it to the cart. The cart stays clear for today’s order, and the saved product is still there after checkout.
- **Recently Viewed and Continue Browsing.** A customer who spends ten minutes narrowing down four air fryers and closes the app can pick up where they left off three days later, without searching again.


Customers who wishlisted converted about 2x as often as those who didn’t. We don’t credit Wishlist with all of that lift, since customers who save products are more interested to begin with. The stronger signal is how they saved: about 40% saved three or more products, and we read that as customers comparing options across visits.


### And then there was Trust


A customer buying a ₹3,000 pair of earbuds takes on more risk than one buying milk. They need confidence at two points: when they choose the product, and when it arrives.


Before the order, we built **Ratings** . For an unfamiliar product, seeing what other customers bought and how they rated it helps make the choice easier.


But trust did not end at checkout.


With a higher-ticket purchase, customers also wanted confidence that what arrived was actually what they had ordered and expected.


**Open Box Delivery** moved that verification to the doorstep. Customers open and inspect the product at the doorstep before accepting the order. If it’s damaged or doesn’t match what they ordered, they catch it there, and don’t have to accept it and then start a return.


Removing the risk of via ratings, and open box delivery


We built each of these for a step in the same purchase. Take a customer shopping for a T-shirt. She has to know Zepto sells T-shirts and see enough of the range to find one she likes. She needs to tell the options apart, see the price she’ll actually pay, and come back later to decide. Then she needs to trust what she orders and what arrives. We spent this year building each of those steps.


### Overall Impact


All the above changes has significantly improved the conversion funnel, and the penetration of these categories on Zepto. Over the past year, search to add-to-cart across these categories rose about 18%. First-time category buyers, the group furthest behind repeat buyers, gained the most.


Search to ATC Funnel Impact


### What we’re working on next


Most of this year went into establishing that these categories need a different experience. The next stretch is about depth.


**Search that adapts to the customer.**


Search picks a layout based on the query. The same query plays out differently by customer: one who has bought in the category scans and picks, while a first-time buyer scrolls further, rewrites the query and leaves more often. We’re building search that adjusts to how well the customer knows the category.


**Getting customers to buy the whole category from us**


Speed built quick commerce, but it doesn’t hold back Electronics or Fashion. A customer buying a weekend gift isn’t counting minutes, and ten-minute TV delivery doesn’t help if nobody is home. We’re working out what else customers need to buy these categories from us by default, such as scheduled delivery, installation, insurance.


**Winning the considered purchase**


Customers buy in these categories rarely, so we grow more through bigger orders than more orders. Many customers buy an accessory from us and the device elsewhere. We’re working on earning the purchase they think hardest about.


**Reviews on the product page**


Ratings tell a customer how buyers scored a product. Before a first purchase, they also want the reasons: whether a T-shirt’s fabric pills after a wash, or how earbuds sound on calls. We’re adding written reviews to product pages, so customers can read what buyers liked and what disappointed them.
